draft.title: Extending interpretations
card: An interpretation is a reader's explanation of what a text means. A text can support more than one interpretation, as long as each one can be backed by the text.
A strong reader tests another person's reading against the text. They look for words, images or events that support it, and for any that do not fit.
A reading is weak when it ignores parts of the text or rests on nothing in it. A reading is not weak just because it differs from yours.
A strong reader also builds on a reading. They keep the part the text supports, then add new evidence or a new angle.
draft.remember: Test a reading against the text, then build on what the text supports.

a.q: Which response best tests a classmate's reading of a text?
opts: Checking the reading against details in the text
Choosing whichever reading most people hold
Dropping the reading because it differs from yours
Accepting the reading because the classmate is confident
a.why: Testing means going back to the text to see what supports the reading and what does not. Choosing the most popular view is tempting, but popularity is not evidence from the text.
a.clue: Where should the evidence for a reading come from?

b.q: In a short story, a girl keeps a cracked teacup on her windowsill. Sam says it shows she is clinging to the past. Jo says it shows she values things that are flawed. Which is the best next step?
opts: Look for details that support or challenge each reading
Decide Sam is right because he spoke first
Decide only one reading can be right and discard the other
Choose the reading that sounds most positive
b.why: Both readings could be supported by the text, so the reader checks each against further details and may combine them. Discarding one is tempting, but a text can support more than one interpretation.
b.clue: Both readings may be possible. What settles how well each one holds up?

a.best: Checking the reading against details in the text

b.best: Look for details that support or challenge each reading
